name: Homosalate
lead: Homosalate (3,3,5-trimethylcyclohexyl salicylate) is a salicylate ester used as an organic UVB filter in sunscreens and in daily moisturisers and make-up with SPF. By absorbing UVB, it helps products prevent sunburn, and US labels state that, used with other protective measures, such sunscreens decrease the risk of skin cancer and early skin aging, so it supports the goal of keeping skin tone and texture youthful [1][2][3].

It absorbs UV at roughly 295 to 315 nm, in the UVB range, and its bulky, oily trimethylcyclohexyl group helps dissolve other filters such as avobenzone in a formula and keeps it from washing out in water. Wikipedia reports that it is found in about 45% of US sunscreens [2][3].

Homosalate is under scrutiny in Europe for possible endocrine activity seen in laboratory assays. Wikipedia reports a June 2021 opinion of the EU's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) finding no sufficient evidence that pure homosalate is an endocrine disruptor in humans, while Grokipedia, an AI-generated summary, states the committee considered it acceptable only up to 0.5% in certain cosmetics [1][2]. The two summaries differ, and readers can consult the committee opinions for details.

Human studies concern absorption and allergy: a 2020 JAMA trial found homosalate in plasma after sunscreen use, and a 2025 review argued that six common filters, including homosalate, show no biologically relevant carcinogenic mode of action [4][5].

chain: Absorbs UVB (about 295-315 nm) in the skin's surface
Less UVB reaches skin cells, so less sunburn and DNA damage
Less sun-driven tanning, pigment change and photoaging over time
More even tone and smoother skin
angle.text: Homosalate is one of the filters that gives a sunscreen or SPF moisturiser its UVB protection, so people who apply such products daily use it as part of keeping their skin from tanning, burning and showing sun damage. It is a supporting ingredient rather than a stand-alone treatment [3][6].

paras: Homosalate is a solubilising UVB absorber added to sunscreens and daytime moisturisers, often alongside avobenzone, octisalate and octocrylene. A US label for a facial moisturiser with SPF lists these four filters and states the product helps prevent sunburn and, with other protective measures, decreases the risk of skin cancer and early skin aging caused by the sun [3].
On T Nation in 2013, a fair-skinned poster who had had a basal cell carcinoma described a sunscreen with homosalate 10%, zinc oxide 7.5% and octinoxate 7.5% as the one he used [7].

Homosalate is made by Fischer-Speier esterification of salicylic acid with 3,3,5-trimethylcyclohexanol, a hydrogenated derivative of isophorone. Its density is about 1.05 g/cm3, it melts below minus 20 degrees C, and it is practically insoluble in water (0.4 mg/L) [2]. The salicylic acid part absorbs UVB, and the hydrophobic ring gives the greasy feel and water resistance [2].

Wikipedia reports a study in which about 25% of the applied dose reached the stratum corneum on the face, 2 to 3 times more than on the back, with no homosalate detected in volunteers' blood or urine [2]. A 2003 study compared skin penetration and SPF of five UV filters according to vehicle [8].

The 2020 JAMA randomized trial enrolled 48 healthy participants, who applied one of four sunscreen products (lotion, aerosol spray, non-aerosol spray or pump spray) at 2 mg/cm2 to 75% of body surface area, once on day 1 and four times a day on days 2 to 4, with 34 blood samples over 21 days. Plasma concentrations of all six active ingredients, including homosalate, exceeded the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold after a single application [4]. A 2023 review of US and EU filters likewise noted that oxybenzone, octinoxate, octisalate, homosalate and octocrylene exceeded that threshold and concluded that human data are limited but known human risks of sunscreen appear minimal [6]. A 2024 study examined homosalate toxicokinetics in humans after dermal application for biomonitoring purposes, and a 2022 paper identified its human exposure biomarkers [9][10].

Laboratory work has reported anti-androgenic activity and estrogenic activity in cell assays [11][12][13][14], and reviews summarise endocrine properties of UV filters [15][16]. Wikipedia notes that no estrogenic effects were seen in juvenile rats given up to 1000 mg/kg subcutaneously for three days, in immature rats fed up to 892 mg/kg daily, or in zebrafish exposed for 96 hours, and states there is no in vivo evidence of human endocrine toxicity [2]. A 2025 review applied a mode-of-action approach to six common filters, including homosalate, and concluded they are not genotoxic and show no evidence of biologically relevant carcinogenic modes of action, with human systemic exposure below biologically active levels; it was written in response to the FDA's request for supplementary data such as rodent carcinogenicity studies [5]. The SCCS in June 2021 found in vivo studies showed no genotoxic, phototoxic or photosensitising effects when applied topically, according to Wikipedia [2].

Homosalate and other UV filters have been measured in Hawaiian coastal water, sediment and coral tissue, on beaches in the Canary Islands, in Japanese rivers and lakes and in aquatic biota [17][18][19][20]. A 2021 mini-review of major organic filters, including homosalate, discussed their occurrence in aquatic environments and endocrine-disruption potentials [21].

In the United States homosalate is part of the OTC sunscreen monograph process. Grokipedia says the FDA proposed the monograph in 1978 and that homosalate entered widespread commercial use in the 1980s; it has not been classified as generally recognised as safe and effective under the newer framework, which calls for additional absorption data [1][6]. A 2023 review counted 17 US-approved and 29 EU-approved UV filters [6].

Wikipedia reports that Symrise challenged a European Chemicals Agency decision requiring animal testing of homosalate and 2-ethylhexyl salicylate and lost at the Court of Justice of the EU, with orders dated 16 July 2021 and 28 May 2024; the BBC reported the outcome on 5 May 2023 [2]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, dates the precursor cyclohexanol's characterisation to 1955 and prototype sunscreen use to the late 1960s [1].

Clinical research consists mainly of absorption and allergy studies. A phase 1 systemic-absorption study is registered with 72 participants [22], and the published JAMA trial enrolled 48 [4]. A 10-person SPF determination study from 2009 is registered, and a 1,000-person European photopatch study examined photoallergy to sunscreen ingredients [23][24]. The 2003 vehicle study compared penetration and SPF of five filters [8]. No trial tests homosalate alone for appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: FDA proposes the OTC sunscreen monograph, per Grokipedia [1].
JAMA trial reports plasma levels of homosalate and five other filters [4].
SCCS opinion on homosalate; Court of Justice orders in the Symrise case [2].
Review of US and EU UV filters; Symrise loses appeal reported by BBC [2][6].
Further EU court order in the Symrise case [2].
Mode-of-action review of six filters, including homosalate [5].

card.summary: A common UVB sunscreen filter whose possible hormone-like activity has led to EU concentration limits and animal-testing demands; human harm has not been shown.
card.note: EU concentration limit; endocrine questions under review.

quick.overview:
Homosalate is a chemical sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVB light and is used to build SPF. It is reported in roughly 45% of US sunscreens.

European regulators have examined it for hormone-like effects seen in lab assays. Summaries disagree on how firm the concern is, and no human harm has been demonstrated in the studies listed.
quick.mechanism: Its salicylate group absorbs UVB and its bulky ring keeps it from washing out in water [2].
quick.risks: It is absorbed into blood after sunscreen use per a 2020 trial. Lab studies report anti-androgenic and estrogenic activity; the EU has set a concentration limit and required further testing, and it has been measured in coastal waters and coral tissue.
